What should you charge for a newsletter sponsorship?

Enter your subscriber count, average open rate, and niche below. This turns those numbers into a price range for each common ad placement — a dedicated send, a primary in-issue slot, a secondary slot, and a classified/text link — using the same cost-per-1000-opens logic newsletter ad marketplaces use, applied to your own list instead of a marketplace's cut-taking listing.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Also self-publishing books to the same list? See the KDP royalty calculator for what a book keeps exclusive versus wide. Also monetizing a social following alongside the newsletter? See the brand deal rate calculator for pricing that channel too. Also running a podcast? See the podcast sponsorship rate calculator for pricing that channel as well.

What this does and doesn't do

This applies commonly cited newsletter-ad-market CPM-per-1000-opens benchmark ranges — wide ranges, by design — to the subscriber count, open rate, and niche you enter. It does not know your specific niche's current market, your list's click-through or conversion history, or what a specific sponsor is willing to pay this week. Treat the output as a starting point for a negotiation, not a quote. See where these benchmark ranges come from and how to use them for more.

Already listed on Paved's marketplace, or thinking about it? See how this free calculator differs from a marketplace listing and its 30% commission.

Tempted to just copy a flat CPM figure from a blog post or a competitor's rate card? See why your own open rate and niche move the price.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a newsletter sponsorship?

It depends on your subscriber count, open rate, niche, and which ad placement you're selling. This calculator applies commonly cited market CPM-per-1000-opens ranges to your own numbers to give a starting price range for a dedicated send, a primary in-issue placement, a secondary placement, or a classified/text link.

Why does this calculate price from opens instead of raw subscriber count?

Sponsors are paying for eyes on the ad, not names on a list. Newsletter ad marketplaces routinely price against opens rather than subscribers, because a 20,000-subscriber list with a 15% open rate reaches fewer real readers than a 5,000-subscriber list with a 50% open rate.

Is this price a guarantee of what a sponsor will pay?

No. It is a starting point for negotiation based on general market ranges, not a quote, valuation, or offer performed on your behalf. Actual rates vary by list quality, click-through history, niche demand, and how much a specific sponsor wants your specific audience that week.

What counts as a dedicated send versus a primary or secondary placement?

A dedicated send is a solo email to your list containing only the sponsor's message — it commands the highest price because it has no competing content. A primary placement is the top ad slot inside your regular issue; a secondary placement is a lower slot in the same issue. A classified or text-link placement is the smallest, cheapest unit, usually a line of text with a link.

newsletter-sponsorship-rate-benchmarks.h.text:
NEWSLETTER SPONSORSHIP RATE CALCULATOR

Where do newsletter sponsorship rate benchmarks come from?

Newsletter ad marketplaces (Swapstack, Paved, Sponsy, and others) and creator-economy write-ups routinely quote sponsorship prices as a CPM against opens — cost per 1,000 opens — rather than against raw subscriber count. That single choice is the most useful thing to borrow from them even if you never list your newsletter on a marketplace at all.

Why opens, not subscribers

A sponsor is paying for a person to actually see their ad, not for a row in your database. A list of 20,000 subscribers with a 15% open rate produces about 3,000 opens per send. A list of 5,000 subscribers with a 55% open rate produces about 2,750 — nearly the same number of real readers, from a list four times smaller. Pricing against subscriber count alone rewards a large, disengaged list over a small, attentive one; pricing against opens does not.

Why the ranges are wide

This calculator's benchmark ranges are deliberately wide — often a 2x spread between the low and high end of the same placement and niche. That is not imprecision; it reflects the real spread in what sponsors actually pay, driven by factors a subscriber-count-and-open-rate calculator cannot see:

  • Click-through history. A newsletter with a proven track record of driving clicks for past sponsors can charge toward the top of the range; a first-time seller usually starts lower.
  • Niche demand. A niche with active buyers competing for placements (say, developer tools or personal finance) supports higher prices than a niche with few sponsors chasing it.
  • Audience specificity. A newsletter read almost entirely by, say, practicing veterinarians is worth more per reader to a veterinary-supply sponsor than a general audience of the same size is worth to anyone.
  • Relationship and timing. A sponsor who already has a good relationship with you, or who needs a slot in a specific week, will often pay above the general range.

Use the low end of the range as a floor you should rarely go below, and the high end as a target to work toward as you build a track record — not as two arbitrary numbers to average.

How to move your ask up from the floor

LeverWhat it does
Share past sponsor resultsClick-through rate or conversions from a prior sponsor (with their permission) is the single strongest evidence a new sponsor can act on.
Sell out placements before dropping priceConsistently sold-out inventory is itself a pricing signal; discounting an unsold slot trains sponsors to wait you out.
Bundle rather than discountAdding a second placement (say, a mention in your next issue too) usually protects the per-send rate better than lowering it.
Re-check your open rate by measurement windowSome platforms report open rate over 24 hours, others over 30 days — compare like for like before quoting a number to a sponsor.

Back to the newsletter sponsorship rate calculator.

vs-guessing-a-flat-rate.html.text:
← Newsletter sponsorship rate calculator

This calculator vs. guessing a flat rate

The fastest way to answer a sponsor's "what do you charge?" is to copy a number — a round CPM figure from a creator-economy blog post, or whatever a bigger newsletter in your niche lists on its own public rate card. It costs nothing and takes ten seconds.

What a copied number carries with it is someone else's audience: their open rate, their niche, and whichever single ad placement they happened to publish a price for. A dedicated send and a classified text link are not the same product, and a newsletter with a 55% open rate is not the same inventory as one with a 15% open rate at the same subscriber count — a flat number can't tell the two apart, but a sponsor doing the math on their own return eventually will.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I have no send history yet — what do I even quote? A market rule of thumb, until you have a few issues of open-rate data.
I know my subscriber count and open rate — what should I charge? This calculator — enter your numbers, get a price range per placement immediately.
A competitor lists $30 CPM. Should I just use that? Only if your open rate and niche happen to match theirs — otherwise it's their audience's price, not yours.
Does a dedicated send really cost more than a classified link? Yes, usually several times more in the same niche — see where the benchmark ranges come from.
Can I get an answer without signing up anywhere? This calculator — a static page, no sign-up, nothing uploaded.
Get a price range now

This tool needs no account and lists nothing: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your subscriber count, open rate, and every computed price stay on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

What's wrong with copying a competitor's rate card?

Their rate reflects their subscriber count, their open rate, and their niche — not yours. Two newsletters with the same subscriber count can have very different open rates, and open rate is what a CPM-per-opens benchmark actually prices against. Copying their number carries their audience quality into your quote, in either direction.

Isn't a round number like $20 CPM close enough?

It can land close by coincidence, but a single flat CPM cannot represent both a dedicated send and a classified text link at once — the calculator's own benchmark ranges price a dedicated send several times higher than a classified slot in the same niche, because the ad gets the whole email instead of one line inside it. A flat number picks one placement's price and applies it to all four.

When is a flat rate the better choice?

When you have no subscriber count or open rate to work from yet — a brand-new newsletter with no send history — there is nothing for this calculator to price, and a market rule of thumb is the only starting point available. Once you have a few issues of open-rate data, your own numbers are the better anchor.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your subscriber count, open rate, and every computed price stay on this device and are never uploaded.

This page names no specific product — it compares against the generic habit of copying a flat rate, not a competing marketplace. See this calculator vs. Paved for how it compares against a marketplace instead, and where these benchmark ranges come from and how to use them.

vs-paved.html.text:
← Newsletter sponsorship rate calculator

This calculator vs. Paved

Paved is a newsletter sponsorship marketplace: you list your newsletter, advertisers browse hundreds of publications by category and audience size, and they book a sponsorship at the price you set (or a rate its Smart Pricing tool suggests from marketplace demand). Paved handles discovery, booking, and payment for a 30% commission on every sponsorship it books.

That makes Paved the right choice for finding advertisers you don't already have, and running the whole booking and payment process through a marketplace. This page answers a narrower question: for a sponsor you already have — your own network, a cold pitch, a returning advertiser — what should you actually charge, free, with no listing and no cut of what you negotiate directly.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I don't have a sponsor yet — where do I find one? Paved's marketplace, or another advertiser network.
I already have a sponsor (or a lead) — what should I quote them? This calculator — enter your numbers, get a price range immediately, nothing listed.
What's a typical range across the whole market, by list size? Paved's published benchmarks, drawn from its own marketplace bookings.
What's a defensible range for my specific subscriber count, open rate, and niche? This calculator's own CPM-per-opens math — see where the benchmark ranges come from.
Can I get an answer without listing my newsletter or giving up a commission? This calculator — a static page, no sign-up, no booking, no cut.
Get a price range now

This tool needs no account and lists nothing: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your subscriber count, open rate, and every other figure stay on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere, there is no marketplace listing, and no commission on whatever you and your sponsor agree to.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Paved?

They solve different problems. Paved is a marketplace: you list your newsletter, advertisers browse and book a spot at the price you set (or Paved's Smart Pricing suggests), and Paved handles discovery, booking, and payment in exchange for a 30% commission on the sponsorship. This page is a free calculator: no listing, no advertiser discovery, no commission. You enter your subscriber count, open rate, and niche, and it gives you a price range to quote a sponsor you already found yourself — through your own network, a cold pitch, or a returning advertiser.

Does Paved price the same way this calculator does?

Not exactly the same inputs, but a similar idea. Paved's own guidance says sponsorship rates vary enormously by reach and reputation — indie newsletters listing spots as low as $100, with market averages cited around $5,000 and larger publications commanding thousands more — and its Smart Pricing tool suggests a rate from marketplace demand data it collects across its network. This calculator has no marketplace data to draw on; it applies commonly cited CPM-per-1000-opens benchmark ranges to your own subscriber count, open rate, and niche instead, so the range is grounded in your own numbers rather than what Paved's advertiser pool happened to book this quarter.

Is Paved free?

Not to publish through. Paved does not charge advertisers a platform fee, but it charges publishers a 30% commission on every sponsorship booked through its marketplace. This calculator has no listing, no booking flow, and takes no cut of anything — it is a free static page that only computes a price range.

Is this page affiliated with Paved?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Paved, and this page is not a review of it. Paved is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is for. The commission and benchmark figures described above are drawn from Paved's own published materials rather than measured by us, and marketplace fees, plans and listing requirements change — check Paved's current terms on their site before relying on any number here.
